content: The 2013 guidelines on HIV testing, antiretroviral therapy (ART), and service delivery provide detailed recommendations for various populations and scenarios. Below is a professional interpretation of the key points: HIV Testing and Counseling 1. Community-Based Testing: In areas with generalized HIV epidemics, community-based HIV testing and counseling, linked to prevention, care, and treatment services, is recommended alongside provider-initiated testing and counseling. This is a strong recommendation, though based on low-quality evidence. Similarly, in all epidemic settings, community-based testing for key populations is also recommended with the same conditions. 2. Adolescents: HIV testing and counseling, with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care, is strongly recommended for adolescents from key populations in all epidemic settings (generalized, low, and concentrated). This recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence. When to Start ART 1. Adults and Adolescents: ART should be initiated as a priority in individuals with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) or a CD4 count ≤350 cells/mm³. ART is also recommended for individuals with a CD4 count between 350 and 500 cells/mm³, regardless of clinical stage. Additionally, ART should be started in all individuals with HIV in the following situations: Active tuberculosis (TB) disease. HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV) co-infection with severe chronic liver disease. HIV-positive partners in serodiscordant couples to reduce transmission. 2. Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women: All pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV should initiate triple ART, at least for the duration of the risk of mother-to-child transmission. Women meeting treatment eligibility criteria should continue lifelong ART. For programmatic reasons, particularly in generalized epidemics, lifelong ART is recommended for all pregnant and breastfeeding women. In some cases, ART may be stopped after the transmission risk period if the woman does not meet eligibility criteria for her own health. 3. Children: ART should be initiated in all children under five years of age with HIV, regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage. For children aged five years and older, ART is recommended for those with a CD4 count ≤500 cells/mm³. ART should also be started in children with severe or advanced symptomatic disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) regardless of age or CD4 count. Infants under 18 months with a presumptive clinical diagnosis of HIV should also start ART. ART Regimens 1. First-Line ART for Adults and Adolescents: The preferred regimen includes two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus one non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). Specifically, a fixed-dose combination of tenofovir (TDF), lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC), and efavirenz (EFV) is recommended. Alternatives include regimens with zidovudine (AZT) or nevirapine (NVP). The use of stavudine (d4T) is discouraged due to its toxicities. 2. Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women: A once-daily fixed-dose combination of TDF, 3TC (or FTC), and EFV is recommended, including during the first trimester of pregnancy. Infants of mothers on ART and breastfeeding should receive six weeks of daily nevirapine (NVP) prophylaxis. For infants receiving replacement feeding, four to six weeks of NVP or twice-daily AZT is recommended. 3. Children Under Three Years: A regimen based on lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) is preferred. If LPV/r is not feasible, a nevirapine-based regimen can be used. For children who develop TB while on ART, a regimen of abacavir (ABC), 3TC, and AZT is recommended during TB therapy, with a return to the original regimen afterward. 4. Children Aged Three Years and Older: Efavirenz (EFV) is the preferred NNRTI for first-line treatment, with nevirapine (NVP) as an alternative. The NRTI backbone should include ABC + 3TC or AZT + 3TC, depending on the child’s weight and age. Monitoring ART Response and Treatment Failure 1. Viral Load Monitoring: Viral load testing is the preferred method for diagnosing and confirming ART treatment failure. If viral load testing is unavailable, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used. Second-Line and Third-Line ART 1. Second-Line ART: For adults and adolescents, second-line regimens should include two NRTIs and a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor (PI). The choice of NRTIs depends on the first-line regimen used. Heat-stable fixed-dose combinations of atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) or LPV/r are preferred PIs. 2. Third-Line ART: National programs should develop policies for third-line ART, which should include new drugs with minimal cross-resistance, such as integrase inhibitors and second-generation NNRTIs and PIs. Patients on failing second-line regimens with no new options should continue a tolerated regimen. Operational and Service Delivery Recommendations 1. Adherence Support: Mobile phone text messages can be used as reminders to promote adherence to ART. 2. Service Integration: ART should be initiated and maintained in maternal and child health settings, TB treatment settings, and opioid substitution therapy (OST) settings, with appropriate linkages to ongoing HIV care. 3. Decentralization: ART initiation and maintenance can be decentralized to peripheral health facilities or community-based settings. 4. Task-Shifting: Trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses can initiate and maintain ART. Community health workers can dispense ART between clinical visits. Guidance for Program Managers National authorities should implement these recommendations through a transparent and inclusive process, considering local HIV epidemiology, program performance, and socioeconomic factors. Ethical, equity, and human rights considerations should also guide decision-making. Drug Interactions The guidelines highlight significant drug interactions, particularly involving antifungal and antiviral medications, and emphasize the need for careful monitoring of renal function and plasma concentrations when certain drugs are co-administered. Herpes Zoster Treatment For herpes zoster, acyclovir is recommended as the first-line treatment, with a dosage of 800 mg five times daily until lesions are fully crusted (usually 7–10 days). Treatment should ideally begin within 72 hours of symptom onset.
